content.text: I think I called him after the first read and was like bruh .... ... I sent the things and then he called me back like why

Anthony Fenech
Tigers beat writer
Detroit Free Press
(734) 752-9667
Twitter: @anthonyfenech
From: Thomas, Christopher <cdthomas@freepress.com>
Sent: Friday, August 23, 2019 3:39 PM
To: Fenech, Anthony <afenech@freepress.com>; Cybulski, Joe <jcybulski@freepress.com>
Subject: New column 
 
It was avoidable and inexcusable.

The Houston Astros knowingly violated the MLB collective bargaining agreement, which is designed to protect reporters and ballplayers, when the franchise blocked Free Press writer Anthony Fenech from entering their clubhouse with Houston media on Wednesday night.
Justin Verlander, arguably the greatest pitcher in Tigers history and now the Astros’ ace, refused to talk to any reporters with Fenech present.  So, the Astros made sure Fenech was absent.
Players have no obligation to talk to every media member in a postgame scrum. They can ignore questions. They can give non-answers.
But the league says reporters must have access.
The Astros know this. They just didn’t care.
The Baseball Writers’ Association of America exists to protect credentialed media from such backlash and retribution. And so does the CBA
That Verlander and Fenech have a checkered past isn’t the issue. Or at least it shouldn’t be.

Yet in the interest of clarity and transparency, it’s important to explain how the relationship ultimately soured. And how the Astros’ decision to block access ultimately started a public relations debacle.
xxxxxxxx
In a tweet Thursday, Verlander said Fenech showed “unethical” past behavior.
It stems from a Sept. 12 interview that went on and off the record and ended with a disagreement about the context surrounding the exchange of Fenech’s phone number.

Fenech had been assigned to ask Verlander about a Bleacher Report story published Aug. 9, 2018, in which Verlander said the Tigers “misdiagnosed” an injury in 2015. The Free Press was the only Detroit media outlet to ask Verlander about the comments, and he didn’t like it.
Verlander later apologized to the Tigers for his characterization of the situation. And in the aftermath, he exiled Fenech from any of his good graces.
Verlander has refused to talk to Fenech since September, and even before that he had refused to answer some of Fenech’s questions in a group setting.
In mid-May, when the Astros came to town, Gene Dias, the Astros’ vice president of communications, called Fenech and told him Verlander would not grant him any interview requests.

Then on Wednesday afternoon -- a day after Verlander walked out of a media availability after Fenech asked a question -- Dias told Fenech that Verlander wasn’t speaking to him because the misdiagnosis story was published in 2018.
Here’s how Fenech says the 2018 interview went down:

Fenech interviewed Verlander in the visiting clubhouse at Comerica Park on Sept. 12 and asked permission to turn on his recorder. Verlander said yes. The conversation alternated on and off the record. He told Verlander he’d return after the game to verify quotes for clarity, which is not a typical practice. 
After the interview, Dias told Fenech that Verlander was having second thoughts about the interview. Dias said he felt that not publishing the story could help Fenech’s working relationship with Verlander in the future. Verlander, according to Dias, deemed the story unnecessary. (NEED TO CALL DIAS)
Fenech returned to the Astros clubhouse to clarify a quote with Verlander, who then said he believed the conversation was off the record. Fenech read the quote to Verlander and said he planned to use it in the story. As another courtesy, he gave Verlander the option to clarify his remarks. The quote read, in part: “I’m going to let it lie. No point in drudging up the past anymore. I think the easiest way for me to answer it is, it was initially diagnosed as a tricep and it ended up being a lat.”
Fenech handed Verlander his business card and told him that if he needed to add to or clarify the quote, he could contact him before the Free Press’ print deadline time. Fenech then told Verlander he wanted to preserve the relationship. It was during this exchange that Verlander’s camp says Fenech crossed the line, with the pitcher feeling as if Fenech was using the story to gain Verlander’s personal cell phone number.  (CALL JV AGENT)
xxxxxxxx

There’s nothing in the MLB collective bargaining agreement that would force Verlander to speak to Fenech. The Free Press understands that. And we understand some stories lead to contention and can affect one-on-one access.
But group access can’t be prejudicial.

When the Astros used three security officials to stand between Fenech and the clubhouse doors while Verlander spoke to reporters inside, it sent a message that the BBWAA is powerless against baseball’s biggest stars. And that a credentialed media member’s access can be revoked just because a player doesn’t like him.

On Wednesday afternoon, Verlander’s camp reached out to the Free Press. His agent, Mark Pieper, left a voicemail on my office phone to discuss Verlander’s issues with Fenech. Regrettably, I didn’t hear the voicemail until Thursday.

Still, the conversation wouldn’t have changed the Free Press’ stance: Fenech needed to be at Wednesday’s game and Verlander’s postgame media session for two simple reasons: He’s our beat reporter. And it’s his job.
Disagreements happen in clubhouses and locker rooms all the time. Not all reporters and athletes get along.
But we ask our journalists to show up every day in the face of any conflict and conduct themselves professionally.
We expect the professionals on the other side to do the same.

Blocking access runs counter to the mission of the BBWAA, which was established in 1908 “to ensure its members have access to players and others in the game so members’ reporting can be accurate, fair and complete.”
Fenech wasn’t asking for a one-on-one interview. He wasn’t asking whether the conversation was on or off the record.
He was asking to participate in a group interview with multiple reporters, who all heard the same comments from Verlander.
The Astros’ decision is inexcusable. Yet  on Thursday, they defended their intentional breaking of the rules as “appropriate” in this isolated case.
The MLB has since contacted the Astros and told the franchise not to block access again.
But that’s not enough.

The Free Press plans to file a formal grievance to the league on Friday. In the grievance, we’ll urge MLB to adhere to its collective bargaining agreement and fully discipline the Astros for breaking the rules.
“Any club whose personnel violate these regulations will be disciplined,” The CBA’s Club-Media Regulations states.
Not because a ballplayer wouldn’t talk to a reporter.
But because the ballplayer’s franchise did not act professionally.
And it didn’t follow the rules.
